content.p: On Thursday 8 July 1982 Saddam Hussein drove into Dujail, a Shia farming town on the Tigris north of Baghdad, on a visit that his personal cameraman filmed. As his convoy left, a small group of local men opened fire on it from the palm groves. The president was unhurt. What followed was a campaign of arrests, torture, deportation, property destruction and executions against the town, which Iraq's own courts would later treat as a crime against humanity.

The reprisals went almost unreported abroad. Twenty-three years later they became the subject of the first trial of Saddam Hussein by the Iraqi High Tribunal. It ended with his hanging and with a sharp dispute over whether a trial so flawed could be called justice.
content.h2: A town on the wrong side of the war
content.p: Dujail sat in a mixed region. CNN noted that it lay in Salaheddin province, which is heavily Sunni, down the river from Samarra and from Saddam's own Tikrit. The BBC called it a mixed town of Sunni and Shia Arabs, while NPR and others described it as predominantly Shia. Reports put its population at about 75,000, though a local account in Asharq Al-Awsat spoke of 4,000 citizens in the area it described.

The timing mattered. Iraq had invaded Iran in 1980, and by mid-1982 the war was turning against Baghdad. NPR's Anne Garrels reported that the town had little love for a leader who had attacked Shia Iran and had cracked down on the banned Shia Dawa Party, which had local support. Ynetnews described Dujail as a refuge for Dawa. The American Forces Press Service, citing prosecutors, said Dawa members were seeking revenge for the killing of hundreds of their colleagues in 1980. Dr Toby Dodge of Queen Mary College, London, told the BBC that an attack on the president while the war went badly was a direct blow to his authority.

Saddam's personal cameraman filmed the visit, and the footage reached the public only on the eve of the 2005 trial. CNN described a man in military dress strolling through streets lined with crowds, declining a glass of water in one house and telling a crowd from the roof of the party headquarters, "I know and everyone knows that the people of Dujail are courageous."

The attack came off camera. A witness named Mohammed Ali told CNN that one of the shooters, Hassan, asked him for a lift on his motorcycle and was carrying two pistols. Another witness, Raad, said three gunmen fired from the left side as the convoy reached the orchards and that the guards fired back. The BBC reported that the gunmen missed and that most were killed by the president's bodyguards. Asharq Al-Awsat's source put the group at no more than a dozen young men.

The footage then shows something unexpected. Rather than leaving, the convoy returned to town, and Saddam told a crowd, "These few shots don't frighten the people of Iraq, and they don't frighten Saddam Hussein." The BBC said he promised to root out a small number of traitors, "agents of foreigners", a reference to Iranians, and was seen questioning two suspects himself. One man answered that he was fasting and on his way home. "Keep them separate and interrogate them," Saddam told his associates.

The Dawa party was later reported to have claimed the attack. NPR noted in 2006 that Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki belonged to the party "that has now claimed to be behind the assassination attempt".

According to NPR, helicopters strafed the area, tanks ringed the town and a curfew was imposed, and the secret police began arrests that spread to anyone rumoured to oppose the government. Ali Abbas Hussein al-Hasaraji, who was 15 at the time, told NPR that his grandparents, three aunts and two young cousins were among more than a thousand people sent to an internment camp in the south, and that two uncles taken to Abu Ghraib prison never came out. The family learned they had been executed only after the 2003 invasion.

The numbers differ. Human Rights Watch's later briefing paper on the judgment recorded a prosecution claim that more than 600 people of both sexes and all ages were detained after the attack and that an unspecified number were tortured. A year later, it said, about 400 of them were sent into internal exile in a remote stretch of the south. Estimates cited by the US military's press service, drawn from rights groups and Iraqi officials, put the arrests at about 1,500. A residents' representative quoted in Asharq Al-Awsat gave 612 men detained from 78 families, said five families lost every male member and said thirteen children were born in jail. An account in the same article spoke of 1,450 of the town's citizens arrested. Survivors there described years in Abu Ghraib followed by years in stone huts in the desert at al-Busayyah, where many died. Saadi Kadhem Jaafar told the BBC that around 150 relatives, his seven daughters and their mother among them, were held at intelligence headquarters for a month, in Abu Ghraib for two years, and then sent to the desert. His brother Karim was one of the gunmen.

The land was targeted too. NPR said bulldozers uprooted the groves of suspects' families and that the palm groves where the shooting took place had become desert. CNN reported that "more than 247,000 acres" of orchards and palm groves were destroyed. The residents' representative quoted in Asharq Al-Awsat gave 16 hectares of arable land destroyed, along with the demolition of the whole al-Wihda district. Those two figures are far apart and the pages do not reconcile them.
content.h2: The 1984 trial and the death toll
content.p: Human Rights Watch summarised what the Dujail case later established. About a year after the arrests, the authorities sent 148 men and boys before the Revolutionary Court, which condemned them to death in 1984 in a summary proceeding. As many as 46 of them died in detention between 1982 and 1984, and the government executed most of the survivors in 1985.

Other sources give different counts. The BBC wrote of 143 people killed. Ynetnews said about 150 were executed, some of them 13-year-olds. The representative quoted by Asharq Al-Awsat said 259 people had died, 143 of them after a single trial and the rest later. NPR reported that some of those sentenced were as young as 11 and were held until they turned 18. Survivors described children whose recorded ages were altered to 25 before execution, according to the Asharq Al-Awsat account. A man named Ali, who was 14 when he and his brothers were jailed, told CNN he later found a document signed by Saddam in 1985 ordering the execution of 149 people from the town, among them seven of his brothers.

Silence followed. Ynetnews said the Economist was one of the few outlets to report on the town in 1982, first on the assassination attempt and later saying Dujail had been erased from the map. It added that the intelligence chief mentioned the attempt in a book some two years later without a word about the reprisals.

After the 2003 invasion Saddam was found hiding in a hole near his home village in December 2003. The Iraqi Special Tribunal, later renamed the Iraqi High Tribunal, announced in July 2005 that its first case would be Dujail. The BBC quoted the law professor Michael Scharf, who helped train its judges, as saying the prosecution picked Dujail because it was its strongest case. Ynetnews offered a blunter reason: a massacre of hundreds is easier to document than one of thousands.

Eight men were charged. According to Human Rights Watch they were Saddam Hussein; his half-brother Barzan al-Tikriti, head of the General Intelligence Directorate from 1979 to 1983; former vice-president Taha Yassin Ramadan; Awad al-Bandar, chief judge of the Revolutionary Court from 1983 to 1990; and four former Baath Party members from Dujail itself. Residents quoted by the American Forces Press Service believed al-Tikriti, Ramadan and al-Bandar organised the retaliation.

The trial opened on 19 October 2005, when Saddam pleaded not guilty. In the following weeks a defence lawyer for al-Bandar was found shot dead and another, for Ramadan, was murdered; the lawyer for al-Tikriti was wounded and left the country. A third defence lawyer was killed in June 2006. One of the five judges stepped down in December 2005, and in January 2006 the chief judge, Rizgar Amin, resigned after Shia politicians complained that he had not controlled the court. Rauf Abd al-Rahman replaced him.

Evidence of what happened came from survivors. One courtroom report described Ahmad Hassan Mohammad, who was 15 in 1982, weeping as he recalled a night at a military police post with 350 others, his 77-year-old father made to watch as his 16-year-old brother was given electric shocks, and the loss of seven of his ten brothers. He quoted an officer shouting, "You people of Dujail, we have disciplined Iraq through you." The same hearing dissolved into shouting, with Saddam telling the judge, "If you want Saddam Hussein's neck, you can have it."

The case against Saddam turned on whether he had personally ordered the killings. Al Jazeera's timeline records that prosecutors presented what they called a signed execution order in February 2006, that on 1 March Saddam accepted for the first time in court that he had ordered the trial of Shia suspects implicated in the assassination attempt, and that experts confirmed the authenticity of his signature on documents in April. Human Rights Watch added that a separate report with margin notes apparently by Saddam was never authenticated, because the court's handwriting experts said they lacked the equipment. Saddam's own defence, in the words of one news report, was that the executed residents had been convicted in a legitimate Iraqi court of trying to kill him.

On 5 November 2006 the court sentenced Saddam Hussein, al-Tikriti and al-Bandar to hang. Ramadan received life imprisonment, three local defendants got 15 years each for aiding and abetting, and Muhammad Azzawi was acquitted at the prosecution's request. Saddam was convicted of wilful killing as a crime against humanity. Reaction split along sectarian lines: NPR described celebrations in Shia areas and angry protests in Tikrit and Ramadi, and Al Jazeera reported the government closing two Sunni television stations.

On 26 December 2006 the Appeals Chamber confirmed the death sentences, calling Ramadan's life term too lenient. Human Rights Watch noted that it reviewed a 300-page judgment in under three weeks. Saddam was hanged on 30 December, in a scene recorded on a mobile phone that showed him taunted on the gallows. Al-Tikriti and al-Bandar were hanged before dawn on 15 January 2007. Human Rights Watch described al-Tikriti's decapitation as apparently inadvertent, and said that Ramadan was executed on 19 March after the trial chamber imposed the death sentence.

Human Rights Watch, one of only two international organisations to monitor the trial regularly, concluded in November 2006 that the proceedings were "fundamentally unfair". Its report listed failures to disclose key evidence to the defence, denial of the right to confront witnesses, lapses in the presiding judge's demeanour and gaps in the evidence. It also said government officials undermined the tribunal's independence from the start.

The group's later review of the judgment criticised how the court inferred knowledge and intent. In al-Bandar's case, it said, the chamber reasoned from his post as chief judge and his membership in the Baath Party. The Bush administration took the opposite view; presidential spokesman Tony Snow said the judiciary was operating independently. Whatever the judgment on the process, the survivors' demand was plain. Ali al-Hasaraji, who survived being pulled off a bus by gunmen looking for people from Dujail, told NPR: "We want justice."
